titre: The blessing the Church withdrew from trial by fire and water
accroche: In 1215, a council forbids priests to bless the judicial ordeals of hot iron and water. Without them, England invents another way to judge.
contenu_vulgarise:
Rome, November 30, 1215, the feast of St. Andrew. At the Lateran, Pope Innocent III presides over the closing session of a council opened on November 11, which brings together, according to surviving counts, 71 patriarchs and metropolitans, 412 bishops and 900 abbots or priors (more than thirteen hundred prelates in all), from across Christendom. The assembly approves decrees drafted in advance: seventy according to the Catholic Encyclopedia, seventy-one canons according to Wikipedia. The eighteenth forbids clerics to pronounce or carry out a sentence of death, to sit as judges in trials of routiers, archers and other men of war given to bloodshed, and, in the same breath, to bless or consecrate judicial ordeals by boiling water, cold water or hot iron.

## A blessing that made up the whole judgment

Until then, across much of Christian Europe, an accused whom neither witness nor confession could sort out submitted to the ordeal: plunging the hand into boiling water, carrying a white-hot iron for a few paces, being immersed with hands bound in blessed water. The outcome, a burn that heals or does not, a body that sinks or floats, counted as a verdict, because it was read as the judgment of God. But this divine judgment could be obtained only through the priest's blessing, which consecrated the ordeal and made it admissible. In withdrawing that blessing, canon 18 does not reform a detail of procedure: it removes from the ordeal the very gesture that made it work as proof.

## A void no one filled all at once

In England, King Henry III has to react quickly: without the ordeal, there is no legal means left to judge accusations of theft, murder or arson. A royal instruction sent in 1219 to the itinerant justices admits it plainly: the question of how to judge these crimes had been left hanging, unresolved before their circuit began, since trial by fire and water had been forbidden by the Roman Church. The text offers no single solution: it authorizes the judges to imprison, banish or release on bail according to their own assessment, leaving them, in the words of one historian of English law, perplexed but free to improvise.

From this improvisation, spread over several decades and never decided all at once, comes the habit of having a jury settle guilt, a role that local juries had already played since 1166 to accuse, but not yet to judge. Legal historian Finbarr McAuley qualifies this too-linear account: the abandonment of the ordeal belongs, in his view, to an older campaign of church reform, aimed at sharply separating the tasks of the clergy from those of the secular world: the council of 1215 extends this movement more than it improvises it. A Roman council, by withdrawing a liturgical gesture, pushed a kingdom to invent, without premeditating it, the ancestor of trial by jury.

citation.texte: Neither shall anyone in judicial tests or ordeals by hot or cold water or hot iron bestow any blessing
citation.source: H. J. Schroeder, Disciplinary Decrees of the General Councils, B. Herder, 1937, pp. 78-127

carte.punch: A council withdraws its blessing from the ordeal. A kingdom improvises, and the ancestor of the jury is born.
carte.idee: In 1215, the Fourth Lateran Council forbids priests to bless judicial ordeals by water and hot iron, stripping them of religious validity. In England, judges, with no legal method for judging crimes and thefts, improvise; the ancestor of trial by jury gradually emerges.

quiz.question: Why does the 1215 ban concretely prevent the practice of the ordeal, rather than merely discouraging it?
choix: Because the council also forbids judicial duels, making any mode of proof by physical ordeal illegal
Because the Church removes from secular courts the right to pronounce a death sentence, making the ordeal pointless
Because the council replaces the ordeal with a jury procedure that it imposes itself on all Christian kingdoms
Because only the priest's blessing made the ordeal valid as the judgment of God, and the canon forbids that gesture
quiz.explication: The ordeal counted as proof only because a priest consecrated it in God's name. The council sets up no replacement procedure, for England or for any kingdom: by withdrawing the blessing, it leaves the ordeal religiously empty, which forced each jurisdiction to find its own solution, like the English jury.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Besides the blessing of judicial ordeals, what else does canon 18 forbid to clerics?
choix: To celebrate Mass in parishes where an ordeal has taken place
To receive gifts from the families of the accused judged by ordeal
To pronounce a death sentence, or to sit as judges in trials of routiers, archers and other men of war given to bloodshed
To travel outside their diocese without the pope's authorization
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Canon 18 forbids clerics to pronounce or carry out a death sentence, to sit as judges in trials of routiers, archers and other men of war given to bloodshed, and, in the same breath, to bless or consecrate judicial ordeals.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when is the closing session of the council that adopts canon 18 held?
choix: At Avignon, in the Palace of the Popes, on November 30, 1215
In Rome, at the Lateran, on November 30, 1215
In England, in Canterbury Cathedral, in 1219
In Rome, in St. Peter's Basilica, on December 25, 1215
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The closing session of the Fourth Lateran Council is held in Rome, at the Lateran, on November 30, 1215 (the feast of St. Andrew), under the presidency of Pope Innocent III, after the opening on November 11 and a second plenary session on the 20th.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what does the royal instruction sent in 1219 to the English itinerant justices allow?
choix: Resuming the ordeal by water, but without the priest's prior blessing
Systematically having the accused tried by a jury of twelve peers
Sending all criminal cases to the church courts
Imprisoning, banishing or releasing on bail, according to their own assessment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The royal instruction of 1219 imposes no single solution: it authorizes the itinerant justices to imprison, banish or release on bail according to their own assessment, leaving them perplexed but free to improvise.
